title: Virology
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 300L Virology curriculum: virus structure and classification (including the Baltimore scheme), viral replication strategies (bacteriophage lytic/lysogenic cycles and general animal virus replication), cultivation and quantification of viruses, medically important human viruses, antiviral chemotherapy and vaccines, and subviral agents (viroids and prions).

questions.question: Viruses are generally distinguished from cellular microorganisms (bacteria, fungi, protozoa) by the fact that viruses:
options: Are obligate intracellular parasites that cannot replicate independently of a living host cell
Possess their own ribosomes for protein synthesis
Have a cytoplasmic membrane and cell wall like bacteria
Can generate their own ATP through independent metabolism
questions.correct_answer: Are obligate intracellular parasites that cannot replicate independently of a living host cell
questions.explanation: Viruses lack the cellular machinery (ribosomes, metabolic enzymes) needed for independent replication and must hijack a host cell's machinery to reproduce, distinguishing them fundamentally from free-living cellular microorganisms.

questions.question: The protein coat that surrounds and protects the nucleic acid core of a virus is called the:
options: Capsid
Envelope
Capsomere alone without further structure
Nucleocapsid core only
questions.correct_answer: Capsid
questions.explanation: The capsid is the protein shell, built of repeating protein subunits called capsomeres, that encloses and protects the viral genome; together with the genome it forms the nucleocapsid.

questions.question: Some viruses, such as influenza virus and HIV, possess an outer lipid membrane derived from the host cell, called the:
options: Envelope
Capsid
Tail sheath
Pilus
questions.correct_answer: Envelope
questions.explanation: Enveloped viruses acquire a lipid bilayer envelope, studded with viral glycoproteins, by budding through a host cell membrane; enveloped viruses are generally more susceptible to inactivation by drying, detergents and lipid solvents than non-enveloped viruses.

questions.question: A complete infectious virus particle, consisting of the nucleic acid genome and its protein coat (and envelope, if present), outside a host cell, is called a:
options: Virion
Prion
Plasmid
Capsomere
questions.correct_answer: Virion
questions.explanation: The virion is the extracellular, fully assembled infectious form of a virus, capable of transmitting from one host cell (or organism) to another.

questions.question: Unlike cellular organisms, the genome of a virus can be composed of:
options: Either DNA or RNA, but never both in the same virion
DNA and RNA together within every virus
Only double-stranded DNA in all cases
Protein rather than nucleic acid
questions.correct_answer: Either DNA or RNA, but never both in the same virion
questions.explanation: Viruses are unique in having either a DNA or an RNA genome (never both simultaneously in the same particle), which may be single- or double-stranded, and linear or circular, depending on the virus family.

questions.question: The Baltimore classification system groups viruses primarily according to:
options: The nature of their genome and the pathway used to produce messenger RNA
Their host range (plant, animal or bacterial)
The geographic region where they were first discovered
Their capsid symmetry alone
questions.correct_answer: The nature of their genome and the pathway used to produce messenger RNA
questions.explanation: David Baltimore's classification system organises viruses into seven classes based on genome type (DNA/RNA, single/double-stranded, polarity) and the specific route each uses to generate mRNA for translation by host ribosomes.

questions.question: In the Baltimore classification system, a positive-sense (+) single-stranded RNA virus is distinguished by the fact that its genome:
options: Can be directly translated by host ribosomes as if it were mRNA
Must first be transcribed into DNA before use
Is identical in sequence to the template strand, requiring transcription before translation
Contains only protein, with no nucleic acid at all
questions.correct_answer: Can be directly translated by host ribosomes as if it were mRNA
questions.explanation: A positive-sense RNA genome has the same sequence (and polarity) as mRNA, so it can be translated immediately by host ribosomes upon entry, without requiring a prior transcription step, unlike negative-sense RNA viruses.

questions.question: Retroviruses, such as HIV, are classified within the Baltimore scheme as viruses that:
options: Use reverse transcriptase to convert their single-stranded RNA genome into DNA
Have a double-stranded DNA genome replicated directly by host DNA polymerase
Package only protein and no nucleic acid
Cannot integrate into the host genome
questions.correct_answer: Use reverse transcriptase to convert their single-stranded RNA genome into DNA
questions.explanation: Retroviruses carry the enzyme reverse transcriptase, which converts their RNA genome into double-stranded DNA that is then integrated into the host cell's chromosome as a provirus, a defining feature of this virus class.

questions.question: The bacteriophage lytic cycle culminates in:
options: Lysis of the host bacterial cell, releasing newly assembled phage progeny
Permanent, harmless integration of phage DNA into the host chromosome
The host cell dividing normally with no phage replication
The phage remaining dormant indefinitely
questions.correct_answer: Lysis of the host bacterial cell, releasing newly assembled phage progeny
questions.explanation: In the lytic cycle, the phage redirects host machinery to replicate its genome and assemble new virions, then triggers lysis (often via phage-encoded lysozyme) to rupture the host cell and release progeny phages to infect new cells.

questions.question: A temperate bacteriophage that has integrated its genome into the host chromosome and remains dormant is called a:
options: Prophage
Virion
Capsid
Envelope
questions.correct_answer: Prophage
questions.explanation: A prophage is the integrated, quiescent form of a temperate phage's genome within the host bacterial chromosome, replicated passively along with host DNA until induction triggers entry into the lytic cycle.

questions.question: The general steps of animal virus replication typically proceed in the order:
options: Attachment, penetration, uncoating, biosynthesis, assembly, release
Assembly, attachment, release, biosynthesis, penetration, uncoating
Release, attachment, uncoating, penetration, assembly, biosynthesis
Uncoating, release, attachment, assembly, penetration, biosynthesis
questions.correct_answer: Attachment, penetration, uncoating, biosynthesis, assembly, release
questions.explanation: The standard animal virus replication cycle proceeds through attachment to a specific host receptor, penetration into the cell, uncoating of the genome, biosynthesis of viral components, assembly of new virions, and finally release from the cell.

questions.question: The initial, highly specific step in which a virus binds to a particular receptor molecule on the host cell surface is called:
options: Attachment (adsorption)
Uncoating
Assembly
Maturation
questions.correct_answer: Attachment (adsorption)
questions.explanation: Attachment is the specific binding of viral surface proteins to complementary receptor molecules on the host cell membrane, and largely determines a virus's host range and tissue tropism.

questions.question: Enveloped animal viruses commonly leave the host cell by a process called:
options: Budding through the host cell membrane, acquiring their envelope in the process
Immediate lysis of the host cell in every case
Direct injection into a neighbouring cell without ever leaving the first cell
Conjugation with a bacterial cell
questions.correct_answer: Budding through the host cell membrane, acquiring their envelope in the process
questions.explanation: Many enveloped viruses assemble their nucleocapsid within the cell and then bud through a region of host membrane modified with viral glycoproteins, acquiring their envelope as they exit, often without immediately killing the cell.

questions.question: Because viruses cannot be cultured on non-living artificial media, they are commonly propagated in the laboratory using:
options: Living host systems such as cell culture, embryonated eggs, or laboratory animals
Standard nutrient agar plates
Selective and differential bacteriological media
Anaerobic broth culture alone
questions.correct_answer: Living host systems such as cell culture, embryonated eggs, or laboratory animals
questions.explanation: Since viruses require living host cell machinery to replicate, they are propagated using cell culture monolayers, embryonated chicken eggs, or susceptible laboratory animals, rather than on the cell-free media used for bacteria.

questions.question: The plaque assay technique used to quantify infectious virus particles relies on:
options: Counting clear zones of dead/lysed cells formed in a cell monolayer, each originating from a single infectious virus particle
Measuring the total protein content of a virus stock
Observing viral particles directly with the naked eye
Weighing the dried virus sample
questions.correct_answer: Counting clear zones of dead/lysed cells formed in a cell monolayer, each originating from a single infectious virus particle
questions.explanation: In a plaque assay, a diluted virus sample is applied to a cell monolayer under a semi-solid overlay; each infectious particle initiates a localized zone of cell killing (a plaque), allowing the concentration of infectious virus (plaque-forming units) to be calculated.

questions.question: A cytopathic effect (CPE) observed in virus-infected cell cultures refers to:
options: Visible morphological changes or damage to host cells caused by viral infection
The formation of bacterial colonies on the culture surface
An increase in the pH of the culture medium
The complete sterilisation of the culture flask
questions.correct_answer: Visible morphological changes or damage to host cells caused by viral infection
questions.explanation: Cytopathic effects, such as cell rounding, syncytium (giant cell) formation, or lysis, are microscopically visible signs of viral damage to infected cells and are used to detect and sometimes tentatively identify viral infection in cell culture.

questions.question: The human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) primarily targets and depletes which type of immune cell?
options: CD4+ T helper lymphocytes
Red blood cells
Platelets
Skeletal muscle cells
questions.correct_answer: CD4+ T helper lymphocytes
questions.explanation: HIV uses the CD4 receptor (along with a co-receptor such as CCR5 or CXCR4) to enter and progressively destroy CD4+ T helper cells, leading to the profound immunodeficiency that characterises AIDS.

questions.question: Influenza viruses undergo frequent minor changes in their surface antigens (haemagglutinin and neuraminidase) through a process called:
options: Antigenic drift
Antigenic shift
Latency
Provirus formation
questions.correct_answer: Antigenic drift
questions.explanation: Antigenic drift refers to the gradual accumulation of point mutations in the influenza surface glycoproteins over time, which allows the virus to partially evade pre-existing immunity and necessitates regular updates to seasonal flu vaccines.

questions.question: Antigenic shift in influenza virus, associated with the emergence of major pandemics, occurs through:
options: Reassortment of genome segments between two different influenza strains co-infecting the same host cell
Gradual accumulation of point mutations over many years
Loss of the viral envelope
Conversion of the virus into a bacteriophage
questions.correct_answer: Reassortment of genome segments between two different influenza strains co-infecting the same host cell
questions.explanation: Because the influenza genome is segmented, two different strains infecting the same cell (e.g., in a pig, a common 'mixing vessel') can exchange whole gene segments, abruptly producing a novel virus with new antigenic properties capable of causing a pandemic.

questions.question: Herpes simplex virus is notable for its ability to establish, after primary infection:
options: Latency in nerve ganglia, with periodic reactivation
Permanent elimination from the body after a single infection
Immediate integration into the host chromosome as a retrovirus
Complete resistance to all antiviral drugs
questions.correct_answer: Latency in nerve ganglia, with periodic reactivation
questions.explanation: Herpes simplex virus establishes lifelong latent infection in sensory nerve ganglia (such as the trigeminal ganglion), from which it can periodically reactivate, causing recurrent lesions such as cold sores.

questions.question: Hepatitis B virus is transmitted primarily through:
options: Blood and body fluids, including perinatal and sexual transmission
Contaminated food and water (faecal-oral route)
Airborne respiratory droplets
Insect bites
questions.correct_answer: Blood and body fluids, including perinatal and sexual transmission
questions.explanation: Hepatitis B virus spreads through exposure to infected blood and body fluids, including mother-to-child transmission during birth, sexual contact, and contaminated needles, distinguishing it from the faecal-oral spread of hepatitis A.

questions.question: Poliovirus, a non-enveloped RNA virus, primarily causes disease by infecting and damaging:
options: Motor neurons in the spinal cord, potentially causing paralysis
Cardiac muscle exclusively
The liver, causing jaundice
Skin keratinocytes only
questions.correct_answer: Motor neurons in the spinal cord, potentially causing paralysis
questions.explanation: Poliovirus can spread to the central nervous system and destroy motor neurons in the anterior horn of the spinal cord, resulting in the characteristic flaccid paralysis of paralytic poliomyelitis in a minority of infections.

questions.question: Rabies virus is transmitted to humans primarily through:
options: The bite of an infected animal, introducing virus-laden saliva
Contaminated drinking water
Airborne transmission over long distances
Sexual contact
questions.correct_answer: The bite of an infected animal, introducing virus-laden saliva
questions.explanation: Rabies virus is present in the saliva of infected animals and is most commonly transmitted through a bite wound, after which it travels along peripheral nerves to the central nervous system, causing fatal encephalitis if untreated before symptom onset.

questions.question: Reverse transcriptase inhibitors, such as zidovudine (AZT), are used in antiretroviral therapy to treat HIV infection by:
options: Blocking the conversion of viral RNA into DNA, preventing viral genome integration
Directly killing infected cells
Preventing the virus from binding to CD4 receptors
Stimulating antibody production against HIV
questions.correct_answer: Blocking the conversion of viral RNA into DNA, preventing viral genome integration
questions.explanation: Reverse transcriptase inhibitors interfere with the reverse transcriptase enzyme's conversion of the HIV RNA genome into DNA, a step essential before the virus can integrate into and hijack the host cell's genome.

questions.question: Neuraminidase inhibitors such as oseltamivir (Tamiflu) treat influenza infection by:
options: Preventing the release of newly formed virions from infected cells
Directly destroying the viral capsid
Blocking viral attachment to host receptors
Inhibiting host cell DNA replication
questions.correct_answer: Preventing the release of newly formed virions from infected cells
questions.explanation: Neuraminidase inhibitors block the viral neuraminidase enzyme, which normally cleaves sialic acid to release newly budded virions from the infected cell surface, thereby limiting the spread of infection to new cells.

questions.question: Live attenuated vaccines, such as the oral polio vaccine, work by:
options: Using a weakened form of the live pathogen that replicates minimally, stimulating strong and long-lasting immunity
Using only a purified viral protein with no live component
Injecting pre-formed antibodies directly
Using inactivated (killed) whole virus incapable of any replication
questions.correct_answer: Using a weakened form of the live pathogen that replicates minimally, stimulating strong and long-lasting immunity
questions.explanation: Live attenuated vaccines contain a weakened version of the pathogen that can still replicate to a limited extent, closely mimicking natural infection and typically eliciting robust, durable immune responses, though carrying a small risk of reversion to virulence.

questions.question: Inactivated (killed) vaccines, such as the injectable (Salk) polio vaccine, differ from live attenuated vaccines in that they:
options: Contain virus that has been chemically or physically killed and cannot replicate in the recipient
Contain fully live, unmodified pathogen
Cannot be used safely in any population
Provide lifelong immunity after a single dose without boosters
questions.correct_answer: Contain virus that has been chemically or physically killed and cannot replicate in the recipient
questions.explanation: Inactivated vaccines use pathogen that has been killed (e.g., with formalin) so it cannot replicate or cause disease, generally requiring multiple doses or boosters to achieve and maintain adequate immunity compared with live attenuated vaccines.

questions.question: Small, infectious, circular single-stranded RNA molecules that lack a protein coat and cause disease exclusively in plants are called:
options: Viroids
Prions
Bacteriophages
Retroviruses
questions.correct_answer: Viroids
questions.explanation: Viroids are the smallest known infectious agents, consisting of a short circular RNA molecule with no protein coat, and are responsible for several economically important plant diseases.

questions.question: Prions, the infectious agents responsible for diseases such as bovine spongiform encephalopathy and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, are unique in that they:
options: Are composed entirely of misfolded protein, with no nucleic acid genome
Contain a large double-stranded DNA genome
Are bacteria that lack a cell wall
Reproduce through binary fission like normal cells
questions.correct_answer: Are composed entirely of misfolded protein, with no nucleic acid genome
questions.explanation: Prions are infectious, misfolded conformations of a normal host protein (PrP) that propagate by inducing normal protein molecules to adopt the same misfolded shape, without any nucleic acid genome -- a radical departure from all other known infectious agents.

questions.question: The capsid symmetry seen in many bacteriophages, combining an icosahedral head with a helical tail, is described as:
options: Complex (binal) symmetry
Purely icosahedral symmetry
Purely helical symmetry
Spherical symmetry with no defined structure
questions.correct_answer: Complex (binal) symmetry
questions.explanation: Many tailed bacteriophages (e.g., T4) display complex or binal symmetry, combining an icosahedral capsid head that houses the genome with a separate helical tail structure used for host attachment and DNA injection.

questions.question: Interferons, produced by virus-infected host cells, help limit viral spread mainly by:
options: Signalling neighbouring uninfected cells to activate antiviral defences
Directly lysing infected cells like a chemical detergent
Neutralising extracellular virus particles like antibodies
Repairing damaged host DNA
questions.correct_answer: Signalling neighbouring uninfected cells to activate antiviral defences
questions.explanation: Interferons are cytokines secreted by virus-infected cells that bind receptors on neighbouring cells, triggering the expression of antiviral proteins that inhibit viral replication and help limit the spread of infection through host tissue.
